sections.h2: Selling in Shaker Heights starts with an inspection
sections.html:
Shaker Heights is a planned inner-ring suburb on Cleveland's eastern edge, and a sale here starts with a city inspection that most Ohio towns do not require. The Point of Sale rule covers every residential sale, so how fast you can sell depends on how soon the inspection can be booked.

Population is 28,466 by the July 2025 estimate, down 3.4% from the April 2020 base, on 6.29 square miles of land. Houses sit close together and many were built in the first half of the twentieth century. Roughly 75 percent of the city's area lies inside the Shaker Village Historic District, a federal historic listing. The city holds houses to its own maintenance chapters in the codified ordinances: Chapter 1411 for residential occupancy and Chapter 1412 for landscaping and yard upkeep.

Typical home value is $303,200, 60.3% of households own, and there are 12,806 households in all. Rent at the midpoint is $1,168 a month.

sections.h2: Point of Sale inspection and who pays
sections.html:
It is a visual interior and exterior inspection the seller must schedule through the city before signing a contract with a buyer, and the seller pays the fee. The application goes in online through the city's CitizenServe system, with payment taken in the same step.

An inspector walks the house, the garage and the yard. For a single or two family home the visit takes about 90 minutes. The city asks sellers to allow at least two weeks from application, and three to four weeks in the busy spring season, so applying before you list is the practical move.

Point of Sale fees charged by the City of Shaker Heights

The Building and Housing Department is at 3400 Lee Road, phone 216-491-1460, with in-person counter service weekdays between 8:30 and 3:30 and phone or email contact until 5 p.m. Permit, license and Point of Sale applications are online only.

sections.h2: What happens if the inspector finds violations?
sections.html:
You get a Certificate of Inspection listing what must be fixed, and you have 90 days to correct the items and book a re-inspection whether or not the house sells. A house with no violations receives a Certificate of Compliance instead, and the property can transfer within 24 months of that first inspection.

If repairs will still be open at closing, the buyer or seller submits an itemized estimate prepared by a registered contractor. The buyer then funds an escrow account at 150 percent of the estimated repair cost, held by the city. The city also reviews requests to swap the escrow for a purchase rehab loan when the buyer will live in the home, and it names the HUD 203(K) program as one example of such a loan.

  • The city grants extensions of the 90-day period when repairs are progressing but unfinished, especially where weather is a factor.
  • A buyer who takes a property at sheriff's sale or another court-ordered auction has 30 days after transfer to obtain the inspection.
  • Violations you dispute or do not understand can be raised with the department, which answers questions on deadlines, extensions and affordability.

sections.h2: Other city inspections on a Shaker Heights house
sections.html:
Beyond the sale inspection, the city runs a standing cycle. Owner-occupied homes receive an exterior review every five years, and rental properties get an interior and exterior inspection every three years. Neighbor complaints trigger their own inspection, and any violation notice carries a compliance deadline.

An older violation notice may already be on file for your address. Ask the Building and Housing Department whether anything is open before you sign a listing agreement or accept an offer.

Buyers here shop by neighborhood. There are nine, each named after one of the original elementary schools: Boulevard, Fernway, Lomond, Ludlow, Malvern, Mercer, Moreland, Onaway and Sussex. Public school students attend the Shaker Heights City School District. Two Greater Cleveland Regional Transit Authority rail lines end in the city: the Blue Line runs down the median of Van Aken Boulevard and the Green Line down the median of Shaker Boulevard. Houses within walking range of a station and a neighborhood school often draw the most interest, so mention both in a listing.

sections.h2: Property taxes when a house sells
sections.html:
Cuyahoga County bills the tax, and the Fiscal Office handles valuation and the Homestead program. Ask the Cuyahoga County Treasurer for the schedule on your parcel so the title company can prorate the bill to the closing date.

The Homestead exemption is open to owners aged 65 and up, those permanently and totally disabled, and certain surviving spouses, with an income limit of $41,000 for the current application and $29,000 of value exempted. The applicant must own and occupy the home on January 1, and the filing deadline is December 31. If the owner sells, the exemption stays with the house for that tax year, but a recipient who buys another home must file again. Taxes and the Homestead program run through the county Fiscal Office at 2079 East Ninth Street in Cleveland, and Homestead questions go to 216-443-7420, option 5.

sections.h2: Where to go for each step
sections.html: Two offices carry most of the work: the city for the inspection and the county for taxes. Start with the city, because the inspection controls the contract date. Book the Point of Sale application first, then call the Building and Housing Department about any open notice, and only after that line up the county tax questions with the title company. Keep the certificate the city issues, because a buyer or lender will ask to see it.

sections.h2: When a cash offer makes sense
sections.html:
A cash offer makes sense when the house carries open violations you do not want to repair before closing. The city allows the buyer to take on all or part of the repair responsibility, so a direct buyer can purchase as is and set up the escrow for the remaining items.

That arrangement still runs through the city. The inspection must be applied for before the contract is signed, the escrow still equals 150 percent of the contractor estimate, and the buyer holds the repair duty after title passes. Compare at least two offers, ask who covers the inspection fee and escrow, and get the closing date in writing before you sign.

faqs.q: Do I need an inspection to sell my house in Shaker Heights?
faqs.a: Yes. The city requires a Point of Sale inspection for residential sales, and the application must be filed before you enter into a contract with a buyer. The fee is $200 for a single-family home.

faqs.q: How long does a Shaker Heights Point of Sale inspection take to schedule?
faqs.a: Plan on at least two weeks from the application date, and three to four weeks in the spring season. The visit itself takes about 90 minutes for a single or two family home.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a Certificate of Compliance and a Certificate of Inspection?
faqs.a: A Certificate of Compliance means the house passed and can transfer within 24 months. A Certificate of Inspection means violations were found and must be fixed within 90 days, even if the house is not sold.

faqs.q: Can a buyer take a Shaker Heights house with violations still open?
faqs.a: Yes, with an itemized contractor estimate and an escrow account for 150 percent of the repair cost. For owner-occupant buyers, the city may accept a purchase rehab loan in place of the escrow.

faqs.q: Who do I ask about property tax on a Shaker Heights sale?
faqs.a: Ask the Cuyahoga County Treasurer and Fiscal Office. They can confirm the due dates on your parcel and any Homestead credit, so the title company prorates the bill correctly at closing.
